# Format: <hint><TAB><member CASE label><TAB>...   (fires if ANY member case fails)
# First line doubles as the foothold; lines are ordered most-fundamental first.

How do you express a number in an arbitrary base? What does one step of the conversion produce, what does it leave for the step after it, and at which end of the output does the digit it produces belong? For a negative number, what must come out before the digits, and should the digits be computed from the value or from its magnitude?

Before converting anything, when is a base even usable? Think about its length, whether the same symbol appears twice, and whether a sign character could collide with the '-' you print for negatives. What should the function do when the base fails these checks?
When the number is zero, what single symbol should come out? Is it always a hard-coded zero digit, or is it whatever symbol sits first in the given base?

The most negative int cannot be stored as a positive int of the same type. If you negate it inside an int, what happens? Can its digits be produced without ever holding its magnitude in a type too small for it on some platform? (What C promises about the width of each type: docs/testing.md, under ilp32.)
